page_hint: Ch 2 §3 — 'Occupancy thresholds' paragraph, final sentence
quoted_clause: the attention portion reads KV cache at an intensity of only ~1–8 FLOP/byte and stays bandwidth-bound at every realistic batch size
observed: The '~1–8' range is unexplained. For the canonical full-MHA FP16 model the attention intensity is exactly 1 FLOP/byte; 8 FLOP/byte corresponds to an 8:1 GQA geometry (attention FLOPs are unchanged by head sharing while KV bytes fall by the sharing factor). The reader cannot tell which end applies to the canonical model, and the range reads as measurement scatter rather than as an architectural dependence.
evidence: Recomputed per decode step per GPU: attention FLOPs = 4 x L x d_model / 8 (TP=8) = 4 x 9,500 x 8,192 / 8 = 38.9 MFLOP; KV bytes = 2 x L x (n_kv x d_head) x 2 / 8. Full MHA (n_kv x d_head = 8,192): 38.9 MB -> AI = 1.0 FLOP/byte. GQA 8 x 128 (width 1,024): 4.87 MB -> AI = 8.0 FLOP/byte.
root_cause: The range was carried from a general note without tying each end to a geometry.
correction: Write it as: 'the attention portion reads KV cache at ~1 FLOP/byte for the canonical full-MHA FP16 geometry (and ~8 FLOP/byte for an 8:1 GQA geometry, since head sharing cuts KV bytes without cutting attention FLOPs) — in either case far below the ~295 ridge, so it stays bandwidth-bound at every realistic batch size.'
acceptance_test: Each end of the quoted intensity range is tied to a named geometry, and the canonical model's value is stated unambiguously.

page_hint: Ch 2 §3 — 'Occupancy thresholds' paragraph, final clause
quoted_clause: the real saturation threshold, which includes KV traffic (~3.01 GB/seq at canonical context per GPU), must be measured rather than read off either subset.
observed: The 3.01 GB/seq figure is the input-only basis (24.1 GB / 8 GPUs), while the slot-counting basis used everywhere else in the book (and in the same chapter's host verdict) is the 9.5K resident basis of 24.9 GB, i.e. 3.11 GB/seq. Mixing the two bases inside one paragraph on KV traffic is exactly the kind of slip the book elsewhere polices.
evidence: Recomputed: 24.1 GB / 8 = 3.0125 GB/seq (input-only); 24.9 GB / 8 = 3.1125 GB/seq (resident). Ch 2's own host verdict uses 24.1 GB and 24.9 GB side by side.
root_cause: The input-only figure was carried over from the KV-total arithmetic without switching to the resident basis used for per-sequence traffic.
correction: State the basis explicitly: '~3.01 GB/seq per GPU at the 9.2K input-only basis (~3.11 GB/seq on the 9.5K resident basis used for slot counting)'.
acceptance_test: Every per-sequence KV figure in the book names its basis (input-only vs resident) at the point of use.

page_hint: Ch 3 §3 — subsection heading 'MoE model representative (Mixtral 8x7B class, [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION])' and its preamble; Table 3-2 caption
quoted_clause: We contrast with a representative MoE model in the Mixtral lineage. The exact parameter split is not always published in vendor model cards; the numbers below are plausibility-checked and flagged.
observed: Two problems. (a) The claim that the parameter split 'is not always published in vendor model cards' is misleading for the model actually being used: Mixtral 8x7B's total and active parameter counts are published by the model author (46.7B total, 12.9B active), and the book's numbers (47B / 12.8B) are within rounding of them. (b) The chapter labels the model [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] while simultaneously using a real named family's published geometry (32 layers, hidden 4096, GQA 8 x 128) for the KV comparison. A reader who knows Mixtral will read the numbers as Mixtral's actuals despite the label; a reader who does not will think the geometry is invented.
evidence: The book's own numbers: 5.7B x 8 + 1.4B = 47B total; 2 x 5.7B + 1.4B = 12.8B active. Published Mixtral 8x7B: 46.7B total, 12.9B active, 32 layers, hidden 4096, 32 attention heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128 — the same geometry the chapter uses for the KV arithmetic.
root_cause: The chapter wanted a worked example that is not the canonical model, and used [ILLUSTRATIVE] to signal that, without noticing that the numbers and geometry are first-party published facts.
correction: Pick one of two honest framings. (i) Cite the model card: relabel the subsection '[1P][FACT] geometry, [canonical scenario][DERIVED] arithmetic' with the Mixtral model card as the source, and state the published 46.7B/12.9B figures alongside the book's rounded 47B/12.8B so the rounding is visible. (ii) Rename the model to a generic '8-expert MoE, 32L/4096H, GQA 8 x 128' and keep [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION], deleting the Mixtral attribution and the claim about unpublished splits. Do not keep the current mixture.
acceptance_test: The provenance label on the MoE geometry matches whether the geometry is a published fact or an invented variant; no sentence claims a parameter split is unpublished for a model whose split is published.

page_hint: Ch 3 §6 — 'One verified 2026 transfer: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next', KV cache bullet
quoted_clause: So per-token KV no longer follows the dense formula, and no KV metric for this model is stated anywhere in this book. Chapter 7 works a configuration-backed version of exactly this two-term budget — Qwen3.8-27B's 16 full-attention layers priced separately from its 48 Gated DeltaNet layers — into its own history-state arithmetic, so we do not re-derive it here.
observed: The sentence 'no KV metric for this model is stated anywhere in this book' is immediately followed by a pointer to a KV metric for a sibling model (Qwen3.8-27B) in Ch 7. The two statements sit in adjacent sentences and read as contradictory. The intended distinction (Flash-Next vs 27B) is not signalled.

Chapter 7 does price the equivalent two-term budget for the sibling Qwen3.8-27B (16 full-attention layers priced separately from its 48 Gated DeltaNet layers); that is a different model and its numbers do not transfer.'

page_hint: Ch 3 §3 — Table 3-3, row 'KV cache per request (9.2K ctx, 8-bit)'
quoted_clause: | KV cache per request (9.2K ctx, 8-bit) | ~12 GB | ~0.6 GB | set by attention shape, not routing: dense 80L/8192H full-MHA = 1.31 MB/token x 9,200 ~ 12.06 GB; the challenger's own 32L/4096H GQA (8 KV-heads x 128) = 0.0655 MB/token x 9,200 ~ 0.60 GB — a dense model with the challenger's shape holds the same ~0.6 GB [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] |
observed: The table's KV row is stated only at 8-bit, while the canonical scenario's declared KV precision is FP16 and every fleet number in the book uses the FP16 figures (24.1/24.9 GB). The FP16 values exist only in the prose ('~24 GB', '~1.2 GB'), so a reader comparing Table 3-3's '~12 GB' with Ch 4's '24.1 GB' for the same canonical request sees an unexplained factor of two. This is the same precision-basis issue as FT-08, seen from the table side.
evidence: Recomputed: dense 9,200 x 2.62144 MB = 24.12 GB (FP16); challenger 9,200 x 0.131072 MB = 1.206 GB (FP16). Table 3-3 shows only 12.06 GB and 0.60 GB (8-bit).
root_cause: The table was built around the quantization variant for the comparison's sake and the canonical precision was left to the prose.
correction: Add a second row 'KV cache per request (9.2K ctx, FP16 — canonical precision) | ~24.1 GB | ~1.2 GB', or convert the existing row to FP16 and move the 8-bit figures to a parenthetical. Whichever is chosen, the row label must state the precision and the canonical precision must be the one the fleet arithmetic uses.
acceptance_test: Every KV figure in Ch 3's tables carries its precision, and the canonical-precision row matches the 24.1/24.9 GB used in Ch 4.

page_hint: Ch 3 §6 — 'One verified 2026 transfer: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next', first bullet
quoted_clause: **125B total / 6B active** (plus a separate 51B of offloadable N-gram embedding parameters), **512 MoE experts** (10 routed + 1 shared per token), and **hybrid attention** — Gated DeltaNet (GDN) on three of every four layers plus Qwen Sparse Attention (QSA) on the fourth.
observed: The chapter's central discipline is total-vs-active, and it asks the reader to apply it to this model, but it never shows how the stated 6B active follows from the stated geometry (512 experts, 10 routed + 1 shared, 125B total, 51B offloadable N-gram). The reader is given two numbers (125B, 6B) and a routing configuration and asked to take the ratio on trust — the exact move the chapter warns against elsewhere ('pause and ask: is this total or active?').
evidence: Arithmetic available to the reader: 125B - 51B N-gram = ~74B of expert + attention mass; 10/512 routed experts is ~1.9% of expert mass, so the ~6B active figure implies a large always-on attention/shared component (~4.5B) that the text does not state. The book does not show this reconciliation, so the 6B cannot be checked against the geometry.
root_cause: The frontier-model figures were imported as first-party constants without the derivation the chapter itself demands of the reader.
correction: Add one line of reconciliation: 'the 6B active is the routed expert mass (10 of 512) plus the always-on attention/shared parameters; the 51B N-gram embedding table is offloadable and is not part of the per-token working set.' If the always-on component is not first-party published, say so and mark the 6B as a first-party figure whose composition the book does not decompose.
acceptance_test: A reader can reconstruct the 6B active figure from the stated geometry, or is told explicitly which part of it the book cannot decompose.

page_hint: Ch 4 §6 'Architecture Consequence' — 'Model selection' bullet
quoted_clause: but the 140 GB footprint means KV cache for 9.2 K context adds ~20–30 GB of GPU memory per request at peak, leaving headroom but not abundance.
observed: The book computes this quantity precisely everywhere else (24.1 GB at 9.2K input-only, 24.9 GB at 9.5K resident) and uses the precise figure for the 17-slot screen, the 436 GB budget and the host counts. Here it degrades to a '~20–30 GB' range, and 'at peak' is undefined (peak of what — context length, concurrency, or traffic?). The reader cannot tell whether the range is a context-length sensitivity band or a rounding of 24.1 GB.
evidence: Ch 4 §6 'Memory planning' in the same chapter: 'giving ~9,200 x 2.62 MB ~ 24.1 GB of initial KV per request; a resident request also holds its 300 output tokens, so the slot-counting basis is 9,500 x 2.62 MB ~ 24.9 GB'.
root_cause: An early draft's approximate figure survived in prose after the chapter's arithmetic was tightened.
correction: Replace with the precise figure and name the basis: 'the 140 GB footprint means KV cache for 9.2K context adds ~24.1 GB of GPU memory per request (~24.9 GB on the resident slot-counting basis), leaving headroom but not abundance.' If a sensitivity band is intended, state the context range it corresponds to (e.g. '~24 GB at 9.2K, ~84 GB at 32K').
acceptance_test: Every per-request KV figure in Ch 4 is a single precise number with a named basis, or an explicitly parameterised range.

page_hint: Ch 4 §6 'Architecture Consequence' — 'Serving configuration' bullet
quoted_clause: On each host, continuous batching (e.g. vLLM) is nearly mandatory under this load to hold the 1.2 s TTFT budget: it reduces queueing and improves utilization under concurrency (it does not shorten a single request's 9.2 K prefill); without admission scheduling, queued prefills can push p95 TTFT past the 2 s ceiling
observed: 'Nearly mandatory' is a strong architectural claim presented without the mechanism that would make it true, in a chapter whose own standard is that every optimization is a hypothesis about which resource it shifts. The text does not show what happens without it: at the canonical 17 resident slots per host, a static batch would prefill 17 x 9,200 = 156K tokens in one pass, which at the host's ~19,800 tok/s planning rate is ~7.9 s — roughly 6.6x the 1.2 s TTFT budget. That single calculation turns the assertion into a demonstrated consequence and shows exactly which resource (prefill compute, serialized behind the batch) is being protected.
evidence: Recomputed: 17 x 9,200 = 156,400 tokens; 156,400 / 19,800 tok/s = 7.90 s vs the 1.2 s TTFT budget and the 2 s p95 ceiling. The book's own host planning rate (~19,800 tok/s at 35% MFU) is the right denominator.
root_cause: The claim was stated as a design conclusion rather than derived from the canonical concurrency, which is the derivation the chapter has available.
correction: Replace 'is nearly mandatory' with the demonstrated version: 'continuous batching (e.g. vLLM) is effectively required at this concurrency: with 17 resident slots per host, a static batch would prefill ~156K tokens in one pass, ~7.9 s at the host's ~19,800 tok/s planning rate — far past the 1.2 s TTFT budget and the 2 s p95 ceiling. Continuous batching (or chunked prefill) is what keeps the prefill burst from serialising behind the whole batch.'
acceptance_test: Every 'required / mandatory / necessary' claim about a serving mechanism in the book is accompanied by the arithmetic that makes it necessary at the canonical operating point.

page_hint: Ch 4 §3 — Table 4-1, 'Quality' row
quoted_clause: | **Quality** | Factual accuracy >85% on enterprise Q&A; reasoning via retrieval; no tool use beyond search API | [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] author-chosen target, set with reference to enterprise retrieval-Q&A benchmark suites (e.g. HotpotQA-style) |
observed: The reference adds a false flavour of grounding. HotpotQA is a multi-hop Wikipedia question-answering benchmark; it does not measure 'factual accuracy on enterprise Q&A', and no enterprise RAG accuracy suite is named. The row is correctly labelled 'author-chosen target', but the parenthetical citation invites the reader to treat >85% as benchmark-anchored. The book's own §6 'Model selection' bullet already concedes that 'factual accuracy still depends on retrieval quality, context, and evaluation' — which is the honest framing.
evidence: The row's own status label says 'author-chosen target'; the cited suite does not measure the stated metric on the stated domain.
root_cause: A familiar benchmark name was used as a gesture toward grounding rather than as a measurement anchor.
correction: Either drop the benchmark reference and keep 'author-chosen target; to be validated on an internal eval set (retrieval recall@k plus answer faithfulness)', or name a real measurement protocol: '>85% answer faithfulness on an internal eval set of ~200 graded questions; retrieval recall@5 >= 90%'. The point is that the target must be paired with the instrument that will test it.
acceptance_test: Every quality target in the canonical scenario names the measurement that will validate it, and no benchmark is cited that does not measure the stated metric.

page_hint: Ch 4 §3 — Table 4-1, 'Traffic' row
quoted_clause: | **Traffic** | ~10 rps average; peaks ~40 rps | [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] declared traffic inputs (~2,000 registered users x one request ~every 200 s ~ 10 rps; peak scaled) — declared, not derived from the user population (walk-through in §4.3); $L_{\mathrm{exec}}$ = λ x $W_{\mathrm{exec}}$ ~ 86 (~344 at 40 rps) is a separate derived quantity. |
observed: The row carries a single [ASSUMPTION] label but contains a derived quantity (the ~86 / ~344 occupancy) inside the same cell. The book's own table-level convention says a derived value carries [canonical scenario][DERIVED], and the row's own text calls the occupancy 'a separate derived quantity'. The label scope therefore contradicts the prose in the same cell.
evidence: Table 4-1's table-level provenance note: 'a value arithmetically derived from those assumed inputs (an occupancy, a tokens-per-second rate, a cost-per-request, a tokens-per-dollar figure) is [canonical scenario][DERIVED]'. The Traffic row's occupancy is exactly the listed example of a derived value.
root_cause: The row was compressed to fit the table and the derived figure was appended to the assumption cell without a second label.
correction: Label the two quantities separately inside the cell: '~10 rps average; peaks ~40 rps [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION] ... ; execution occupancy ~86 (~344 at 40 rps) [canonical scenario][DERIVED]'. Apply the same treatment to any other row that mixes an input with a derived figure (the Economic row mixes several).
acceptance_test: Every cell in Table 4-1 that contains a derived figure carries a [DERIVED] label on that figure, distinct from the [ASSUMPTION] label on the inputs.

page_hint: Ch 1 §1 'Concept' — 'Tokenization' subsection
quoted_clause: [1P][FACT] A high-frequency English word is often one token (verifiable on most vendor tokenizer demos — e.g. common words like *the*, *we*, *run* render as single tokens); a rare technical term, a long digit string, or dense code is frequently several.
observed: [1P] means first-party — a vendor's own specification or artifact for that vendor's product. The clause generalises across vendors ('most vendor tokenizer demos') and the supporting evidence is a demo page, not a specification. The claim is true but its provenance label overstates it: the first-party artifact supports the claim for one vendor's tokenizer, not for 'most' tokenizers.
evidence: The book's own axis definition (Ch 4 Note 1): '[1P] first-party (vendor spec, method paper)'; '[2°] reputable second-hand (textbook, survey, independent benchmark)'.
root_cause: A verifiable-in-practice claim was labelled with the strongest available provenance rather than the accurate one.
correction: Either relabel as [2°] (a cross-vendor generalisation supported by vendor demos and tokenizer documentation), or make it first-party and specific: '[1P][FACT] In the canonical model's tokenizer, common English words such as *the*, *we* and *run* are single tokens (verifiable on the model card's tokenizer demo); the pattern is typical of byte-level BPE vocabularies [2°].'
acceptance_test: Every [1P] label in the book is attached to a claim about one identified first-party artifact, and cross-vendor generalisations carry [2°].

page_hint: Ch 1 §1 'Concept' — 'KV cache as a concept' subsection, the vLLM FP8-KV sentence
quoted_clause: the vLLM FP8-KV blog post's often-quoted '54%' — from its Llama-3.1-8B Table 3 (vLLM blog, post dated 2026-04-22; retrieved 2026-11-15) [S6] — is, on this book's reading, a decode inter-token-latency (ITL) slope, not a memory ratio or footprint coefficient.
observed: Two issues. (a) The citation key '[S6]' does not match the book's citation style: every other source in the chunk is an inline markdown link with a title and URL (e.g. '[Wan2.2 sampling loop](https://github.com/...)', '[Expert Parallel Deployment](https://docs.vllm.ai/...)'). A bare '[S6]' is unresolvable from the page and forces a trip to the sources section for a claim the reader is being asked to accept against the vendor's own framing. (b) The claim is a strong reinterpretation of a vendor's published number, and the text gives the reader no basis for it beyond 'on this book's reading'. A reader who has seen the blog quoted elsewhere will want to know what the vendor actually plotted.
evidence: Citation style survey across the chunk: inline links at Ch 2 (Wan2.2 x2), Ch 3 (Wan2.2, vLLM expert-parallel docs), Ch 3 ('source: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B', 'source: Meta via vLLM-Recipes'). '[S6]' is the only bracketed numeric key.
root_cause: The citation was drafted against a numbered source list that the manuscript does not use, and the interpretive claim was written without its supporting evidence.
correction: Convert to the book's inline-link style with the URL and the specific table reference, and state the evidence for the reading: e.g. 'the vLLM FP8-KV post's Table 3 reports ITL against batch size for FP16 vs FP8 KV on Llama-3.1-8B; the '54%' is the slope of that ITL curve, not a memory ratio — on this book's reading [1P][FACT] ([vLLM FP8 KV cache blog](url), Table 3, post dated 2026-04-22, retrieved 2026-11-15)'. If the reading cannot be evidenced from the post itself, downgrade the claim to an explicitly labelled [HYPOTHESIS].
acceptance_test: Every citation in the book is resolvable from the page (inline link with title and URL) or is a key that is defined in a numbered list the reader can find; the reinterpretation of the '54%' figure states what the vendor actually measured.

page_hint: Ch 3 §6 — 'Why the trend signal should not be read as "dense is dead"' and 'One verified 2026 transfer: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next'
quoted_clause: **Qwen3.8-27B** ([1P][FACT], source: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B) is a dense 27.8B model whose 4-bit weights fit on a single 24 GB consumer GPU, and **Muse Glimmer 30B** ([2°][FACT], source: Meta via vLLM-Recipes) is a dense 29.6B local-agentic model that runs in ~18 GB at ~5-bit weights.
observed: Two citation-hygiene problems in the same sentence. (a) 'source: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B' is a bare model-card reference with no URL, unlike the inline links used elsewhere in the book; a reader cannot verify it from the page. (b) 'Muse Glimmer 30B' is attributed to 'Meta via vLLM-Recipes' and labelled [2°], but the underlying artifact is a first-party model card from the model's author; the house convention prefers primary sources where a primary source is readily available, and a recipe repository is a secondary restatement of a first-party claim. The [2°] label is honest but the sourcing choice is not the best available.
evidence: The book's own convention (Ch 4 Note 1): '[1P] first-party (vendor spec, method paper)'; '[2°] reputable second-hand'. Elsewhere the book links primary sources inline (Wan2.2 repository at a pinned revision, vLLM expert-parallel docs).
root_cause: Frontier-model citations were added from working notes rather than from the book's citation standard.
correction: Give both models inline links to their first-party model cards and label them [1P][FACT]; if a figure (e.g. the ~18 GB at ~5-bit figure) comes only from the recipe, split the claim: the parameter count and architecture from the model card [1P][FACT], the memory footprint from the recipe [2°][FACT], each labelled separately.
acceptance_test: Every model-specific factual claim in Ch 3 carries an inline link to a first-party artifact, and any figure that exists only in a secondary source is labelled [2°] on its own.

page_hint: Ch 2 §5 'Common Mistakes' — second bullet; compare Ch 4 §5 ('Ch 1 §5's') and Ch 4 §6 ('Ch 2 §1')
quoted_clause: **Assuming one H100 suffices for 70B inference.** The arithmetic in §2.3 shows that a single H100 cannot hold or stream the whole 140 GB model
observed: The book uses two incompatible styles for internal references: '§2.3' (Ch 2) and '§2.2' (Ch 2 Architect's Question) versus 'Ch 1 §5's', 'Ch 1 §4', 'Ch 2 §1', 'Ch 3 §6, Ch. 18'. Under the 'Ch.S' reading, '§2.3' resolves to Ch 2 §3 (Worked Example) and is correct; under the ordinary 'section 2.3' reading it resolves to nothing, because Ch 2 has no §2.3. A reader who reads it the ordinary way is sent to a nonexistent location.
evidence: Reference inventory in the chunk: '§2.2 and Ch 8' (Ch 2 Architect's Question), '§2.3' (Ch 2 §5), '§4.3' (Ch 4 §6), '§6' (Ch 4 §3), '§4.3' (Ch 4 §3), 'Ch 1 §4', 'Ch 1 §5', 'Ch 2 §1', 'Ch 3 §6', 'Ch 4 Table 4-2'.
root_cause: Two reference conventions were used in drafting and neither was declared.
correction: Standardise on 'Ch N §M' everywhere (the form already used for cross-chapter references) and change '§2.3' to 'Ch 2 §3' and '§2.2' to 'Ch 2 §2'. Within-chapter references may keep the bare '§M' form only if the chapter is unambiguous from the page.
acceptance_test: Every internal reference resolves under the book's single declared convention, and no reference uses a dotted '§C.S' form that could be misread as a subsection number.

page_hint: Ch 1 §8 'End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: The Internal Q&A Tool, From First Principles'
quoted_clause: From the token-level work alone (which we worked through in this chapter), the architect can already establish: the unit is tokens; the request shape will be prompt + retrieved context + output; the working hypothesis is input-heavy (Ch 4 quantifies it); and the first number to lock down is tokens-per-request, because every downstream decision (which model fits, how much memory, what latency is possible) is priced against it.

It restates the chapter's conclusions in the architect's voice. By the book's own standard for mini-cases — a decision, evidence, competing interpretations, a calculation that resolves it, and an architectural consequence — this one does not exercise the reasoning it is meant to consolidate. The chapter's own §4 Measurement section supplies the obvious missing exercise: run the model's tokenizer on representative prompts.
evidence: Compare Ch 3's mini-case (computes the residency delta, separates the two accounting lines, refuses the challenger with reasons) and Ch 4's mini-case (new scenario, Little's-law sizing, prefill cross-check, explicit non-contradiction with the canonical case). Ch 1's mini-case has no calculation.
root_cause: The mini-case was written as a scene-setting bridge to Ch 4 rather than as an exercise of Ch 1's content.
correction: Give the architect a concrete token-counting task with a finding that changes a number: e.g. 'the architect runs the candidate model's tokenizer over 200 sample queries and finds the mean prompt is 1,340 tokens, not the 1,200 assumed — and that 12% of queries contain a 20K-token pasted document, so the context distribution has a tail the mean hides. The canonical 9.2K input assumption is replaced by a measured distribution, and the KV budget must be sized against the tail, not the mean.' That single exercise exercises tokenization, the input/output split, the peak-vs-average measurement habit, and the KV consequence, and it hands Ch 4 a measured input rather than a declared one.
acceptance_test: Each chapter's mini-case contains at least one calculation or measurement the reader must perform, and the outcome changes a number the chapter established.

page_hint: Ch 2 §8 'End-of-Chapter Mini-Case: TTFT and the Prefill/Decode Split'
quoted_clause: From the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 alone, the architect can already state the hard numbers: each request carries ~9.2K input tokens and ~300 output tokens. At 10 rps average, the system must sustain ~92,000 input tokens/s in prefill and ~3,000 output tokens/s in decode. [...] The architect can also state the two opposite bottlenecks: prefill will be compute-bound (~1.29 PFLOP per request at 9.2K input), and decode will be bandwidth-bound (a ~140 GB/token weight-read requiring ~5.6 TB/s sustained over each ~25 ms decode step
observed: The sentence attributes the whole set of numbers to 'the unit-and-token work of Ch 1 alone', but the numbers that follow include 1.29 PFLOP and 5.6 TB/s, which are Ch 2's own derivations, not Ch 1's. The misattribution is small but it obscures the chapter's actual teaching move — that the token counts from Ch 1 become FLOP and bandwidth demands only after Ch 2's model is applied.
evidence: Ch 1 contains no FLOP or bandwidth arithmetic; Ch 2 §3 derives both.
root_cause: The mini-case's opening sentence was written to bridge Ch 1 to Ch 2 and then the paragraph was expanded with Ch 2 content without updating the attribution.
correction: Rewrite the opening: 'From Ch 1's token counts and Ch 2's cost model, the architect can state the hard numbers: ...' and, better, make the bridge explicit by showing the two-step derivation (tokens -> FLOPs/bytes -> regime) rather than presenting the results as a single block.
acceptance_test: Every mini-case's attribution of a number to a chapter matches where that number is actually derived.

page_hint: Ch 2 §1 'Concept' — 'Figure convention (used throughout the book)' paragraph
quoted_clause: Arrows in the diagrams carry different meanings by context, and the reader should not assume one universal reading: a **data-flow** arrow (Fig 2.1, 11.3) shows tokens or activations moving; a **dependency** arrow shows "must be decided before"; an **influence** arrow (Fig 4.1) shows "constrains/informs"; a **causation** arrow (Fig 6.1) shows "drives / causes"; and a **conceptual-association** arrow (App. A.4) shows "relates to." Where a figure's arrows are ambiguous, the caption states the intended reading.
observed: The convention list has no category for control flow, yet Fig 2.1's caption distinguishes exactly that: 'The initialize path (labelled initialize) seeds the loop with the first sampled token', and the surrounding prose calls it 'the green initialize path'. A reader applying the stated convention will read the initialize arrow as data flow (tokens moving) when it is sequencing/control (the loop's initialisation). The list also omits the 'append'/'write' arrow used in Fig 1.2 ('written (append) and read (read past K,V, the backward read arrow from the KV cache back to attention)').
evidence: Fig 2.1 caption and Ch 2 §1 prose both name the initialize path as a distinct arrow type; Fig 1.2's caption names a backward read arrow and an append operation; neither maps to the five listed categories.
root_cause: The convention list was written from the figures that existed when it was drafted and was not extended when the KV-cache and pipeline figures were added.
correction: Extend the list: 'a **control/sequencing** arrow (Fig 2.1's initialize path) shows ordering or loop initialisation, not data movement; a **state-write** arrow (Fig 1.2's append) shows persistent state being updated; a **state-read** arrow (Fig 1.2's backward read) shows persistent state being consumed.' Then state the convention once in the front matter rather than inside Ch 2 §1, where it currently competes with the concept material.
acceptance_test: Every arrow type used in any figure maps to a named category in the book's figure convention, and the convention is stated once in the front matter.

page_hint: Ch 4 §3 — Table 4-1 table-level provenance note; canonical box 'Assumption-change log'; Table 4-2 'Note 1'; Table 4-2 table-level provenance note
quoted_clause: *(Table-level provenance — applies to every row unless a row overrides inline. The convention: an input or parameter assumption (traffic, latency target, price, token count) is [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]; a value arithmetically derived from those assumed inputs (an occupancy, a tokens-per-second rate, a cost-per-request, a tokens-per-dollar figure) is [canonical scenario][DERIVED]; ...)* [...] **Note 1 (Table 4-2) — the three label axes, and why the change log does not mix them.** Axis 1 **provenance** ... Axis 2 **epistemic status** ... Axis 3 **measurement status** ... *(Table-level provenance for Table 4-2 — the one convention this chapter and the book uses: one label from the provenance axis and one from the epistemic axis per value, with the measurement status riding along. ...)*
observed: The label taxonomy is restated four times within a single chapter section (Table 4-1 note, the canonical box's change log, Note 1, Table 4-2's note), and the book says it is also defined in the Preface and in 'Sources, Method, and Reproducibility'. Five statements of one convention inside the first chapter the reader meets it is a cognitive tax and a contradiction risk: the four statements are not worded identically (the Table 4-1 note omits Axis 3; Note 1 adds the 'a hypothesis is tagged [HYPOTHESIS], never [ILLUSTRATIVE]' rule; the change log adds the four-state given -> derived -> hypothesized -> validated narrative).
evidence: Four distinct statements of the same convention in Ch 4 §3, plus two external locations cited by the chapter itself.
root_cause: Each artifact was made self-contained, at the cost of repeating the taxonomy; no single canonical statement was designated.
correction: Designate one canonical statement (Note 1 is the natural home, or the Preface) and have every other location point to it with only the delta: e.g. in Table 4-1's note, 'Provenance and status labels follow Note 1 below; this table's rows are all canonical-scenario inputs and derived values, with the inline overrides marked.' Keep the change-log narrative in the canonical box but strip its re-definition of the axes.
acceptance_test: The label taxonomy is defined once in the book; every other mention is a pointer plus a local delta, and no two statements of it differ in wording or content.
